title: The Alpine Kleptomaniac
pageTitle: Living with kea: Sharing spaces with an inquisitive parrot (kea conflict guide)
quote: Kea love chewing on rubber and seats. ... Kea like to chew on rubber-coated wires, especially on things like tractors and solar panels. ... Kea also like the texture of soft rubber washers ... If kea are getting at the rubber around your chimney flue ... When kea have access to rubbish or food, they quickly learn to scrounge.
correctedFact: Kea have a serious rubber habit. New Zealand's Department of Conservation says these inquisitive parrots love chewing on car rubber and seats, and they also go after rubber-coated wiring on tractors and solar panels, soft rubber roof washers and the rubber around chimney flues.
note: DOC supports rubber chewing on cars and food scrounging; no credible page found for ski resorts, tourists, or stolen gloves and wallets (DOC Treble Cone kea video page is retired, NZ On Screen summary says only that kea get over-enthusiastic with cars).

title: Recycling Its Own Shell
pageTitle: Cherry Shrimp Neocaridina davidi (Bouvier 1904) (Crustacea: Decopoda: Atyidae)
quote: As with all arthropods, Neocaridina davidi grows by molting their exoskeleton (Figure 5). They will feed on their molted exoskeleton to reabsorb valuable nutrients.
correctedFact: Nothing goes to waste when a cherry shrimp molts. Like all arthropods, it grows by shedding its exoskeleton, and then it turns around and feeds on the cast-off shell to reabsorb the valuable nutrients still locked inside it.
careAdvice: Experienced keepers leave a fresh molt in the tank for a day or two rather than removing it, giving the soft new shell underneath a real head start on hardening.
note: The page says nutrients, not calcium or minerals specifically, and says nothing about keepers or the new shell hardening faster.

title: Needs Salt Water to Be Born, Dies From It as an Adult
pageTitle: Dietary effects of phytoplankton and zooplankton on larval survival, duration and growth of four Caridina species (Decapoda: Caridea: Atyidae) under laboratory conditions
quote: C. multidentata larvae had prolonged larval durations under limited nutritional conditions, suggesting their ability to broadly disperse in the sea. ... larvae moulted to juveniles after reaching the threshold size of each species needed to migrate to their adult freshwater habitat.
correctedFact: Amano shrimp spend their childhood at sea. Their larvae spread out in the ocean, and when food runs short they can stretch that larval stage out longer, which may help them travel far. Only after reaching a threshold size do they become juveniles and head for the fresh water where adults live.
note: The adult half (a small dose of salt kills adults) was not found on any credible page; searches turned up only adult tolerance data for other Caridina species (up to about 80% seawater for 48 hours, not opened) and a retailer claim, so the title's adult claim looks doubtful but is not proven wrong.

title: Same Shelf, Different Families
quote: Palaemonetes paludosus (Gibbes, 1850) ... status: unaccepted ... valid name: Palaemon paludosus ... Order: Decapoda; Family: Palaemonidae; isFreshwater: 1
correctedFact: Ghost shrimp and cherry shrimp are not the cousins they look like. The grass shrimp Palaemonetes paludosus, the species usually sold as ghost shrimp, belongs to the family Palaemonidae, while cherry shrimp and Amano shrimp both sit in a separate family, Atyidae.
note: Atyidae for cherry shrimp is from the UF IFAS EDIS page title (IN1301) and for Amano shrimp from the Crustacean Research 2021 paper title (genus Caridina, Atyidae); no credible page found tying the trade name ghost shrimp to P. paludosus (only hobby sites); the convergent-lifestyle claim is unsupported and was cut.

title: The Snake That Builds a Nest
publisher: BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), by herpetologist Romulus Whitaker
pageTitle: It's nearly 1.5 metres wide and 55cm high and houses one of the longest, most venomous animals in the world
quote: The female king cobra is the only snake species to build a nest for her eggs. ... She then spends several days gathering leaves into a pile, sweeping them together with her body ... she begins compacting the pile into a waterproof chamber by repeatedly crawling over it (a completed nest stands nearly a metre high). ... Female king cobras often stay on their nests for the entire incubation period of 75 to 100 days
note: Every detail is on the page, but the same page also says nests measure up to 55 cm high at the centre, which sits uneasily with nearly a metre.

title: Born Blank, Colored by Cold
publisher: Animal Genetics (Yu et al. 2019, open access, PMC)
pageTitle: Mocha tyrosinase variant: a new flavour of cat coat coloration
quote: Cats have TYR variants causing the temperature-sensitive colorations of the sable Burmese (cb cb) and the points of the Siamese (cs cs) ... These amino acid changes apparently reduce enzymatic activity in warmer regions of the animal's body, such as the torso. Full coloration is displayed at cooler regions, such as the ears, face, paws and tail, leading to the term 'points' of the Siamese cat. ... Siamese kittens (cs cs) would be nearly white with only black ears, paws, face and paws (points).
correctedFact: A Siamese cat's coat runs on a thermostat. Its version of the pigment enzyme tyrosinase works poorly in warm parts of the body like the torso, so full color only shows where the body runs cooler: the ears, face, paws and tail. Siamese kittens look nearly white apart from those dark points.
note: The paper confirms the temperature-sensitive enzyme and nearly white kittens with dark points, but does not describe kittens being born white and the points darkening after birth.

title: The Eyes That Bleed on Command
pageTitle: Short-horned lizard: The inflatable 'horny toad' that squirts toxic blood from its eyes
quote: When threatened, they squirt a stream of blood from their eyes up to a distance of 5 feet ... While it doesn't appear to deter birds, the blood does affect canines like dogs (Canis familiaris), coyotes (Canis latrans) and foxes (Vulpes), which shake their heads to get rid of it. The blood is laced with toxic chemicals, which may come from the venomous harvester ants (Pogonomyrmex) that the lizards eat. Although their blood isn't poisonous, it tastes unpleasant to predators.
correctedFact: When a coyote, fox or dog gets too close, a horned lizard can squirt a stream of blood from its eyes up to 5 feet. Canines shake their heads to get rid of the foul-tasting spray, which may get its kick from the harvester ants the lizard eats. Birds don't seem to be put off at all.
note: Ant origin is only a possibility (may come from), not established; Live Science is a science news outlet, not on the preferred list, and writes about the greater short-horned lizard; WCS blog (blog.wcs.org, cached) separately supports canids and a stream up to six feet.

title: The Shiba Scream
pageTitle: Is the Shiba Inu the Right Breed for Your Lifestyle?
quote: They are a vocal breed and can make for good watchdogs. Prospective owners should note that their “unique” vocalizations can cause stress for both the Shiba and themselves.
correctedFact: Shiba Inus have a sound all their own. The American Kennel Club calls them a vocal breed and puts their "unique" vocalizations in quotation marks, warning that these noises can stress out the Shiba and its owner alike. So much for the strong, silent type.
note: No club or kennel page names the Shiba scream or ties it to nail trims, baths or vet visits; the cut grooming point is supported by AKC fun facts ("spend a lot of time grooming themselves and tend to be extremely clean", cached).

title: The Rotten Nest Trick
pageTitle: The Bird That Paints Its Eggs With Bacteria
quote: But during breeding season, a female hoopoe's uropygial gland becomes exceptionally large, and it makes a weird dark brown fluid that smells of rotting meat. This is the stuff that discolours the eggs. ... By filming nesting females, they confirmed that the birds actively paint their eggs with their uropygial secretions. ... Hoopoe nestlings can defend themselves by squirting streams of faeces at intruders
correctedFact: Hoopoe moms paint their eggs with stink. In breeding season a female's preen gland swells and pumps out a dark brown fluid that smells of rotting meat, which she smears onto her eggs. The goo is full of bacteria, and researchers found evidence the birds use them to protect their young before they even hatch.
note: Egg coating, rotting meat smell and chicks squirting faeces at intruders are all on the page; that the smell fends off predators is not, so it was cut along with the droppings point.
